nota_resistencia: Simple average of the published tests we found (Mikel, 2026-11-20: «when you find two or three references, put the average and that's it»). It varies a lot with the condition of the line and how the knot is tied.

fichas.para: Tie the line to a hook, a lure or a swivel.
fichas.resumen: One of the easiest and most reliable hook knots. It works especially well with braid, which tends to slip in other knots.
pasos: Double about 15 cm of the end of the line and pass the doubled line through the hook eye.
With the doubled line, tie a loose overhand knot, leaving the hook hanging from the loop.
Pass the whole hook through the loop that is left.
Wet the knot and pull the main line and the tag end at the same time until it seats on the eye.
Trim the tag end, leaving a few millimetres.
fichas.ojo: The hook or lure has to pass through the loop: with big lures or treble hooks you need a long loop and it is awkward.

fichas.para: Tie the line to a hook, a lure or a swivel.
fichas.resumen: The classic hook knot for thin and medium nylon. Quick to tie without looking.
pasos: Pass the end of the line through the hook eye.
Make five or more turns with the tag end around the main line.
Pass the tag end through the small loop left next to the eye.
Then pass it through the big loop that has just formed.
Wet it and tighten by pulling the main line; trim the tag end.
fichas.ojo: Not recommended with thick lines (over about 30 lb breaking strain): it is hard to tighten properly. With thick line four turns may be enough.

fichas.para: Tie to hooks and swivels, make loops and, doubled (one on each line), join two lines.
fichas.resumen: A knot for almost everything: you can tie on the hook, make a sliding loop or, by tying one on each end, join two lines (the «double uni»). It works with braid and with nylon.
pasos: Pass the tag end through the eye and bring it back parallel to the main line, forming a loop.
Make four to six turns with the tag end around both lines, inside the loop.
Wet it and pull the tag end to close the turns.
Slide the knot down to the eye by pulling the main line; trim the tag end.
To join two lines (double uni): overlap the ends, tie a uni with each one around the other and pull both lines so they come together.
fichas.ojo: As a line-to-line join it is somewhat weaker than the same knot tied to a large eye; to join braid to a fluorocarbon leader, the FG is slimmer and passes better through the guides.

fichas.para: Join the braid main line to a fluorocarbon or nylon leader.
fichas.resumen: The most used braid-to-leader join in spinning and jigging: very slim and strong, and it passes through the guides without catching when casting.
pasos: Keep the braid tight (for example, held in your mouth or on the rod with the drag locked).
Cross the leader over the braid and wrap the braid around the leader, alternating over and under, about twenty times.
Without releasing the tension, finish with several half hitches of the braid around the leader.
Wet it and tighten hard by pulling both lines; trim the leader tag end.
Finish with a few half hitches of the braid on itself and trim.
fichas.ojo: It is hard to learn: the details matter and you have to keep the braid tight the whole time. Better to practise it at home before going out.

fichas.para: Join lines of different type or thickness: nylon to braid, or braid to wire.
fichas.resumen: A simpler alternative to the FG for joining two different lines.
pasos: Double the end of the thicker line to form a loop.
Pass the thinner line through the loop.
Wrap it ten or twelve turns around both legs of the loop, working towards the tip.
Bring the tag end out through the loop, on the same side it went in.
Wet it, tighten by pulling both lines and trim the tag ends.
fichas.ojo: Only moderately easy to tie; the turns must sit neatly, without riding over each other.

fichas.para: Make a small loop at the end of the leader, to change leaders loop to loop.
fichas.resumen: A small loop that sits in line with the line: used to attach and change leaders or rigs without cutting.
pasos: Make a first loop with the tag end, passing it behind the main line.
Make a second loop in front of the first.
Pass the tag end between the two loops.
Push the second loop through the first.
Tighten by pulling the second loop and the main line; trim the tag end.
fichas.ojo: It is easier to tie in the hand than with the hook already on.

fichas.para: Tie the leader directly to the hook shank, for natural bait.
fichas.resumen: The line comes out in line with the hook shank, which helps the hook set. It was created for spade-end hooks (no eye) and is still widely used with bait.
pasos: Pass the end of the leader through the eye (or lay it against the spade), leaving a good length of tag along the shank.
Form a loop along the shank.
Make five to seven tight turns around the shank and the line, from the eye towards the bend.
Hold the turns and pull the main line to close them.
Tighten by pulling the line and the tag end; trim the tag end.
fichas.ojo: The turns must sit together on the shank, without crossing.

fichas.para: Tie the line to a hook or lure.
fichas.resumen: A hook knot that keeps the line's strength very well. It works with nylon, braid and fluorocarbon.
pasos: Pass the tag end through the eye and leave plenty of tag.
Wrap the tag end around both lines (the main line and the tag itself) towards the eye.
Pass the tag end through the first loop, next to the eye.
Then pass it through the loop that has just formed at the top.
Wet it and tighten by pulling the main line; trim the tag end.
fichas.ojo: The thicker the line, the fewer the turns: about seven or eight with thin line and about three with thick line. Do not let the turns ride over each other.

fichas.para: Make a loop in the middle of the line, standing out at a right angle, to hang an extra hook (paternoster, bottom rigs).
fichas.resumen: The basis of multi-hook rigs: each loop stands off the line and the hook does not tangle with the main line.
pasos: Make a big loop at the point on the line where you want the dropper.
Wrap one side of the loop over the other several times (five to seven), leaving a gap in the centre.
Push the centre of the big loop through that gap.
Hold the loop that comes out and pull both ends of the line to close it.
Adjust the size of the loop before fully tightening.
fichas.ojo: The loop should not be very long: it tangles and twists more. With nylon, the knot changes shape as you tighten it; that is normal.

fichas.para: The traditional line: a single filament of polyamide.
fichas.resumen: Cheap, easy to knot and stretchy. It is the most versatile and the one almost everyone starts with.
como_es: It stretches quite a lot: it cushions the fish's head shakes and forgives mistakes on the strike, but transmits bites less well.
It almost floats (density close to that of water): it stays on the surface or sinks very slowly.
It absorbs some water and sunlight degrades it: over time it loses strength. It is worth changing it every season.
It has memory: if it stays on the spool for a long time it comes off in coils.
It resists abrasion reasonably well, but less than fluorocarbon of the same diameter.

colores.para: The most discreet in clear water.
Blends with the bottom and the water; discreet and a little easier for the angler to see.
Easy to see from above the water to follow the line and spot bites, but the fish sees it more too: best with a clear leader.

usos_costa: Main line for surfcasting and bottom fishing from the beach.
Float fishing: it floats and helps keep the float in place.
General-purpose leaders when the water is somewhat coloured.
Shock leaders and tapered lines for powerful casts.
usos_embarcacion: Cheap main line for bait fishing at anchor and on the drift.
Surface trolling, where the stretch cushions sudden runs.
General-purpose leaders.
fichas.ojo: Check it every trip: if the line feels rough or fuzzy when you run your fingers along it, cut that section off. Sun and salt age it even when it is not used.

fichas.para: An improved nylon: a blend of two or more types of nylon in a single filament.
fichas.resumen: It handles like nylon but stretches less and resists abrasion better. It costs a bit more.
como_es: It stretches less than normal nylon: a bit more sensitivity without losing the cushioning.
Better resistance to abrasion and sudden jerks than a nylon of the same diameter.
It is just as easy to knot as nylon.
It floats or sinks slowly, like nylon.

colores.para: Discreet in clear water.
Discreet and a little more visible to the angler.
To follow the line; a clear leader is advisable.

usos_costa: Main line for light spinning and float fishing when you want a bit more sensitivity than with nylon.
Leaders and shock leaders on rocky ground.
usos_embarcacion: Main line for fishing at anchor and on the drift over hard ground.
General-purpose leaders.
fichas.ojo: It is more expensive than nylon and, like nylon, it degrades in the sun: store it in the shade.

fichas.para: A fluoropolymer (PVDF) filament designed mainly for leaders.
fichas.resumen: It is the line that is least visible underwater, it sinks and it stands up very well to abrasion from rocks and shells. Its natural place is the leader.
como_es: It bends light almost like water does (refractive index ~1.42 compared with 1.33 for water and ~1.5–1.6 for nylon): that is why it is less visible. It helps, but it does not make it invisible.
It sinks (it is quite a lot denser than water): it takes the bait and the leader down towards the bottom.
It is the most abrasion-resistant for the same diameter.
It does not absorb water and stands up well to the sun: it lasts longer than nylon.
It is stiffer and harder to knot: always wet the knot before tightening.

colores.para: It is almost always used like this: it is what people buying fluorocarbon are after.
Some brands tint it for particular bottoms or waters; the advantage is debated.

usos_costa: Leaders for bass, white seabream, gilthead bream and other wary fish in clear water.
Leaders on rock, mussel beds or shells, where nylon gets cut.
Shock leader in surfcasting over hard ground.
usos_embarcacion: Leaders for jigging, spinning and fishing at anchor in clear water.
Leaders for wary species and for fishing over rock.
Heavy leaders against teeth that are not very sharp when you do not want to use wire.
fichas.ojo: As a main line on the reel it is heavy, sinks and has memory: it is almost always used only as a leader. It is expensive; buy leader spools, not main-line spools.

fichas.para: Several polyethylene fibres braided (4, 8 or more) into a single line.
fichas.resumen: Very thin and very strong for its diameter, it hardly stretches: you feel everything. It needs a nylon or fluorocarbon leader.
como_es: It hardly stretches: it transmits bites and the bottom instantly and sets the hook better at distance.
Much thinner than a nylon of the same strength: it casts further and wind and current drag it less.
It floats.
It is rated by PE number (higher means thicker) as well as by kilos.
X4 (4 fibres): rougher but more abrasion-resistant. X8 (8 fibres): rounder and smoother, casts further but frays sooner on rock.
The sun does not affect it the way it affects nylon, but it frays with sideways abrasion.

colores.para: Discreet: the most used in spinning.
Visible from far away: to follow the line, see bites on the line and cast at night with a torch.
To know how much line has gone out: each colour is 10 m. Some also have a mark every metre. Designed for vertical fishing.

usos_costa: Spinning with lures: the main line is almost always braid.
Long-distance surfcasting, with a nylon or fluorocarbon shock leader.
Bottom fishing where feeling the bite matters.
usos_embarcacion: Jigging and slow jigging, with multicolour braid to know the depth.
Vertical bottom fishing and drifting in deep water: thin line bows less in the current.
Spinning and popping from the boat.
fichas.ojo: Always with a leader: it is very visible and sideways abrasion against rocks cuts it. Do not tie braid with nylon knots (it slips): use a palomar or FG. It cuts your fingers if you grab it while a fish is pulling.

fichas.para: Steel wire leaders, single-strand or braided, sometimes nylon-coated.
fichas.resumen: For toothy fish that cut through any line: conger eel, bluefish, barracuda, sea pike or shark.
como_es: No toothy fish can cut it.
It is stiff and visible: some fish get wary and the lure loses some of its action.
Coated braided wire is more flexible; single-strand wire is stiffer and thinner.
It kinks and frays: check it after every fish.

colores.para: The classic; it shines underwater.
More discreet; the one recommended in clear water.

usos_costa: Bottom fishing for conger eel from rocks, harbours and breakwaters: wire leader, or very heavy nylon if you prefer the fish not to notice it so much.
Spinning and bottom fishing when bluefish or other toothy fish come in.
A short length (about 15–30 cm) in front of the lure or hook.
usos_embarcacion: Conger eel over rock and wrecks, with a wire or very heavy nylon leader.
Trolling and spinning for toothy predators (barracuda, sea pike, shark).
Short leaders above the lure, joined with a swivel or snap.
fichas.ojo: Use it only when there are teeth: otherwise it scares fish and costs you bites. For conger, many anglers use very heavy nylon (130 lb and up) instead of wire: they cannot cut wire, but if the fish swallows the hook wire does it more harm; with nylon, check for abrasion after every fish.

fichas.para: A braid with a lead core inside that makes the line sink on its own.
fichas.resumen: For trolling in mid-water or near the bottom without using leads or diving planers.
como_es: It changes colour every 10 yards (about 9 m): you count how many colours are out.
Rule of thumb: each colour goes down about 1.5 m at slow trolling speed (about 4 km/h); it changes a lot with speed and lure.
It is thick and very visible: it needs a long nylon or fluorocarbon leader.

colores.para: To work out the depth the lure is running at.

usos_costa: Not used from the shore.
usos_embarcacion: Bottom and mid-water trolling from a boat.
Always with a long leader (several metres) of nylon or fluorocarbon.
fichas.ojo: The colours are a guide, not a measurement: with current or more speed the lure rises. Check on the echo sounder whether you are touching the bottom.

Bass Pro: lead core guide

fichas.para: Which line colour to use depending on the water and what you want to see yourself.
fichas.resumen: Colour is a balance between you seeing the line and the fish not seeing it. The usual solution: a visible main line and a clear leader.
como_es: The fish mainly sees the part close to the bait: that is why the leader matters more than the main line.
In clear water, clear fluorocarbon is the least visible.
In coloured water or at night, colour matters much less.
The idea that red disappears underwater is debated: some divers say it looks black.

colores.para: Leaders in clear water and for wary fish.
Discreet main line for clear water.
Main line to see bites and follow the line; always with a clear leader.
Knowing how much line has gone out (vertical fishing and trolling).

usos_costa: Surfcasting: visible-coloured main line to see the line and a clear leader.
Spinning in clear water: green or grey braid with a fluorocarbon leader.
usos_embarcacion: Jigging: multicolour braid with a fluorocarbon leader.
Trolling: the long clear leader is what the fish sees.
fichas.ojo: There are no conclusive studies on which colour each species sees: take this as a practical guide, not a rule.

fichas.para: The hooks are on short snoods above the lead, which sits at the very bottom.
fichas.resumen: The most used bottom rig: it carries several baits at once and keeps them off the bottom.
como_es: The lead goes at the end; the snoods come off the rig body with swivels, beads or knots.
It carries one, two or three hooks: more baits, more scent in the water.
When it bites, the fish feels the weight of the lead and often hooks itself.
Sliding variant (running paternoster): the rig body runs on the main line and the fish feels less.
medidas: Two-hook surfcasting rigs are usually about 170–180 cm in total, with snoods of about 70 cm.
Short snoods tangle less when casting; long ones move the bait more in the current.
Snoods a little thinner than the rig body: if you snag, only one breaks.
usos_costa: Beach surfcasting: the beach rig par excellence.
Clean or mixed ground for white seabream, gilthead bream, sand steenbras, flatfish and similar.
On very rocky ground, better with a weak link for the lead (so the lead breaks off and not the whole rig).
usos_embarcacion: At anchor and on the drift: several hooks at different heights off the bottom.
Mixed bottom fishing (red seabream, pandora, horse mackerel…).
fichas.ojo: With strong wind and long casts, long snoods tangle: use bait clips to hold them during the cast.

fichas.para: The lead runs freely on the main line, above a swivel; below it goes the hook length.
fichas.resumen: The fish takes the bait and swims off without feeling the weight of the lead: for big, wary fish.
como_es: A running lead (or a clip with a lead) runs on the main line; a bead protects the knot at the swivel.
The hook length comes off the swivel, usually with a single hook.
Positive bite: the line runs through the lead and shows on the rod tip.
medidas: A hook length of 1 to 1.5 m to start with on the beach.
More current, longer hook length: the bait moves more naturally.
Just enough lead to hold the bottom in whatever current there is.
usos_costa: Bass, gilthead bream and big fish from the beach or rocks.
Night bottom fishing with big baits.
Conger eel from harbours or rocks (with a cut-resistant leader).
usos_embarcacion: At anchor in deep water for big bottom fish (conger eel, pollack, rays).
Slow drifting with a single big bait.
fichas.ojo: If the lead is too light, the current drags it and the hook length wraps around the main line: go up in lead before lengthening the hook length.

fichas.para: A rig in which the lead and the hook travel together on the cast and, when the fish bites, the lead rises above it.
fichas.resumen: It casts far and protects the bait during the cast; when the hook is set, the lead moves away from the fish and snags less on rock.
como_es: The rig body runs through a swivel (the «pulley») attached to the main line.
On the cast, the hook is held against the lead with a clip: more distance and the bait does not break up.
While playing the fish, the lead stays above and rises over the rocks.
medidas: Around one rod length in total; the hook length, from 60 cm to 1 m.
Heavy rig body (abrasion-resistant) and a slightly thinner snood.
usos_costa: Long-distance surfcasting on clean beaches.
Ground with rock or weed for big fish: the lead snags less on the retrieve.
usos_embarcacion: Rarely used from a boat: when fishing vertically it is not needed.
fichas.ojo: The rig works doubled over: check the rig body for wear at the swivel every few fish.

fichas.para: The bait hangs from a float at the depth you choose; a stop knot on the main line sets how far it goes down.
fichas.resumen: For fishing in mid-water or close to the rocks without snagging: white seabream, bass, mullet, ballan wrasse, mackerel…
como_es: Fixed float for shallow water (up to 1.5–2 m) or a sliding float with stop knot and bead for deeper water.
Shot under the float until only the tip shows: that way you notice even the most delicate bite.
The final hook length is usually thinner than the main line.
medidas: Depth: start at one metre and go deeper until they bite; for ballan wrasse, the bait should brush the bottom.
A bigger float the rougher the sea and the deeper the water.
Final hook length of 50 cm to 1 m.
usos_costa: Breakwaters, harbours and rocks: in mid-water next to the weed.
Mullet and other species in calm water, with a small float.
Bass with live bait under the float.
usos_embarcacion: At anchor or on a slow drift next to the rocks, with a float.
Mackerel and horse mackerel in mid-water.
fichas.ojo: The tide changes the depth: readjust the stop knot regularly.

fichas.para: A lead on the main line, a swivel that stops it and a leader with a hook behind.
fichas.resumen: The lead drags along the bottom and the bait or soft plastic floats a little above it: very good for bottom fish that look upwards.
como_es: Bullet or barrel lead running on the main line, a bead and the swivel.
Leader with one hook; natural bait or soft plastic.
Cast it and retrieve very slowly, dragging the lead.
medidas: Short leader (about 15–30 cm in the guides consulted) to keep the bait close to the bottom; longer so it moves more.
Lead according to depth and current.
usos_costa: Flatfish (sole, turbot) and other bottom fish on sand, with a slow retrieve.
Soft plastic fishing from the beach and from rocks with clean ground.
usos_embarcacion: Slow drifting over sand for flatfish.
fichas.ojo: On rock it snags a lot: it is a clean-ground rig.

fichas.para: A rig with many small hooks dressed with feathers or flash; the lead goes at the bottom.
fichas.resumen: Used to catch live bait (mackerel, horse mackerel, sardine, bogue…) when there are shoals.
como_es: 6 to 10 small hooks on short snoods.
It needs no bait: the flash is enough; some anglers add a small piece.
Lower it to the shoal and lift and drop it gently.
medidas: Just enough lead for it to drop slowly through the shoal: with too much lead it goes through the shoal too fast.
More lead if it tangles: the rig stays tighter.
usos_costa: Harbours and breakwaters when mackerel or horse mackerel come in.
To get live bait for bass or squid.
usos_embarcacion: Over shoals marked on the echo sounder.
Before going out to fish with live bait.
fichas.ojo: Lots of hooks together: it tangles and pricks. Unhook with pliers and keep it on its winder. Respect minimum sizes with bait fish too.

fichas.para: A length of fluorocarbon or nylon between the braid and the lure.
fichas.resumen: It protects against abrasion, hides the braid and adds cushioning: braid never goes straight to the lure.
como_es: It is joined to the braid with a slim knot (FG or Albright) and to the lure with a knot or a snap.
Fluorocarbon in clear water or around rock; nylon if you want more stretch.
If there are teeth, a short length of wire at the end.
medidas: Length: the knot with the braid should not go into the guides when casting (or it should pass through them as a very slim knot).
Clear water, longer leader; coloured water, it can be shorter.
Thickness: a leader stronger than the braid is pointless; around rock, a little thicker.
usos_costa: Spinning for bass, bluefish and other predators from the shore.
Fishing with soft plastics and stickbaits on rock: the leader is what rubs.
usos_embarcacion: Spinning and jigging from the boat.
Popping for tuna and big predators with a heavy leader.
fichas.ojo: Check the last few centimetres after every fish or snag: the leader gets nicked and it is the first thing to break.

fichas.nombre: Leader thickness and length: how to choose
fichas.para: Practical rules for choosing leader diameter and length depending on the water, the bottom and the fish.
fichas.resumen: The leader is what the fish sees and what rubs: thinner gets more bites, thicker holds more. You look for the balance.
como_es: Thinner than the main line (or snoods thinner than the rig body): if something breaks, let it be only the leader.
Fluorocarbon is slightly thinner than nylon of the same strength.
With rock, shells or fish with hard scales or spines, thicker.
More current, longer leader so the bait moves naturally.
medidas: Beach surfcasting: final fluorocarbon hook lengths of 0.30–0.35 mm are common for medium-sized fish.
Clear water and wary fish: thinner, longer leader.
Coloured water or at night: you can go thicker without losing bites.
usos_costa: Clean beach: thin leader.
Rock and mussels: thick leader or fluorocarbon.
Toothy fish: wire or very heavy nylon.
usos_embarcacion: Rocky bottom: thick snoods.
Very clear water in summer: thin and long.
fichas.ojo: These are guides, not rules: the condition of the line and the knot matter more than the exact diameter.

fichas.nombre: Hook sizes: how they are numbered
fichas.para: How to read a hook number and why a size 2 is not the same in every brand.
fichas.resumen: Up to size 1, the higher the number, the smaller the hook. After that come the «aughts» (1/0, 2/0…), where the higher the number, the bigger the hook. And almost all of us fish with hooks that are too big.
como_es: Order from small to large: … 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 1, 1/0, 2/0, 3/0, 4/0…
1/0 comes after 1; 4/0 is quite a lot bigger than 1/0.
Wire thickness is marked with «X»: a 2X is thicker and stronger than the standard hook of its size.
There is no standard between brands: a size 2 from one brand may differ from another's. If there is no number, look at the gap (the distance between the point and the shank).
medidas: Choose the size by the fish's mouth and the size of the bait, not by the size of the fish.
The bait must leave the point free: if it covers it, the hook is too small for that bait.
usos_costa: Small baits (thin worm, bits of prawn): high numbers (6–8).
Medium baits for white seabream, gilthead bream or bass: around 2 to 1/0 in commercial rigs.

pasarse: Size is chosen by the fish's mouth and by the bait, not by what the fish weighs. A 2 kg gilthead bream has a small mouth and is caught on a small hook; what changes with weight is the wire thickness (a «strong» or 2X hook of the same size), not the number.

A hook that is too big does not fit fully into the fish's mouth: it bites, feels the metal and drops it, or does not even take it. With live bait it is worse: the weight of the hook stops it swimming and the hole kills it sooner.
Going a little too small can be fixed (more bites, the odd one gets away); going too big leaves the rig with no bites. If in doubt, one size smaller.
Quick rule: the bait has to cover the hook, leaving the point free. If you need a huge bait to cover the hook, the hook is too big.

fichas.nombre: Swivels: which one to use when
fichas.para: Quick guide to choosing between the types of swivel.
fichas.resumen: A swivel joins two lengths of line and lets them turn separately, so the line doesn't twist. There are five families and each has its place: you don't need the most expensive one for everything.
como_es: Barrel: the basic one. Joins main line and rig or holds the lead. Turns little under load.
Rolling (ring type): the most used at sea. Turns better than the barrel and is stronger for its small size.
Ball-bearing: turns freely even under heavy load. For anything that spins a lot: spinners, trolling, baits that spin.
With snap or clip: any of the above with a clip to change lure, lead or rig without cutting.
Three-way (T): three eyes; for snoods and multi-hook rigs.
medidas: Choose the smallest one that matches the breaking strain of the rig (or a little more).
Sizes are not the same across brands: check the kilos on the pack, not the number.
For trolling, it should hold at least 1.5 times the line's strength.
usos_costa: Surfcasting: rolling swivel with snap for the lead, and rolling or three-way swivels for the snoods.
Spinning: snap only (no swivel) with swimming lures; rolling or ball-bearing swivel with spinners.
Float fishing: small rolling swivel between main line and leader, which also acts as a stop for the shot.
usos_embarcacion: Anchored and drift fishing: three-way or rolling swivels on snood rigs.
Trolling: ball-bearing swivel with snap; this is where the line twists most.
fichas.ojo: A swivel is also a weak point and a flash the fish can see: use one only where needed and just the right size.

fichas.nombre: Spinning lures: which one for the sea conditions
fichas.para: Which lure family to use depending on the state of the sea.
fichas.resumen: The state of the sea decides: in calm, clear water, surface lures and light soft plastics; in foam and rough sea, lures that grip the water or get down below the foam.
como_es: Calm sea and clear water: stickbait, small popper, floating minnow or unweighted soft plastic.
Rough sea with foam: a minnow that “bites” the water, sinking pencil, soft plastic on a jig head or a somewhat larger stickbait.
Headwind: sinking pencil or casting jig, which fly and cut through the wind.
Coloured (murky) water: white soft plastics or lures with a strong silhouette at different depths; very noisy surface lures usually do poorly.
Very rocky or weedy ground in calm conditions: unweighted soft plastic rigged weedless.
medidas: 9 to 15 cm and 10 to 30 g covers almost all shore fishing for bass.
More weight if it's windy or you need to reach far; less if the fish are tight to the shore.
usos_costa: Bass on rock and beach: the basic box is a stickbait, a minnow, a sinking pencil and a couple of soft plastics with heads of different weights.
Mackerel, bluefish and Atlantic bonito: casting jig or spinner.
usos_embarcacion: Spinning under birds (mackerel, Atlantic bonito, bluefish): casting jig or sinking pencil.
Casting at the rocks from a boat: the same as from the shore.
fichas.ojo: No lure works every time: if nothing happens in half an hour, change lure family before colour.

fichas.nombre: The rod: parts and how to read its specs
fichas.para: What each part of a rod is and what the numbers printed on it mean.
fichas.resumen: Every rod has the same parts: the blank, the guides, the reel seat and the handle. What changes between a surfcasting rod and a jigging rod is the length, power, action and casting weight.
como_es: Blank: the rod's tube (carbon, fibreglass or a mix). Carbon is lighter and more sensitive; fibreglass is tougher against knocks.
Guides (rings): carry the line; the inner ring must be smooth, with no cracks.
Reel seat: where the reel screws in; different for spinning or overhead reels.
Handle: cork or EVA; long on casting rods for leverage.
Tip: the last section; shows the bite.
Power: the force needed to bend it (light, medium, heavy): set by the size of the fish and the line.
Action: where it bends. Fast: only the tip (sensitive, sets the hook quickly). Moderate or slow: bends right down (more forgiving, cushions more).
Casting weight (e.g. 10–40 g or 100–200 g): the weight of lure or lead it casts well. Outside that range it casts badly or can break.
Sections: spigot/put-in joints (better action) or telescopic (easy to carry).
medidas: Long rod: casts further. Short: more accurate and more power to fight.
The rod's casting weight must cover your lures or leads.
usos_costa: Surfcasting: long and powerful.
Spinning: medium and sensitive.
usos_embarcacion: Boat: shorter and more powerful.
fichas.ojo: Don't cast above the casting weight marked on the rod: it's the most common way to break it.

fichas.para: Types of reel and what each spec means: size, ratio and drag.
fichas.resumen: At sea two are mainly used: the spinning reel, easy and universal, and the overhead (multiplier) reel, stronger for boat fishing and trolling.
como_es: Spinning (fixed spool): the spool doesn't turn; the line comes off the front. The easiest, and the one used for surfcasting and spinning.
Overhead (multiplier, “boat reel”): the spool turns; more power and stamina for boat fishing, heavy jigging and trolling.
Spool: holds the line; surfcasting spools are long and tapered to cast far.
Drag: lets line out when the fish pulls harder than the line can take. Front (finer and stronger) or rear.
Ratio (e.g. 5.7:1): turns of the rotor per turn of the handle. But how much line you retrieve also depends on the spool diameter.
Bail arm (pick-up): the arm that winds the line onto a spinning reel.
medidas: Size (1000, 2500, 4000, 10000…) is not the same across brands; within a brand, a higher number is bigger.
In the specs, look at the maximum drag and the line capacity.
usos_costa: Spinning: medium-sized spinning reel.
Surfcasting: large long-spool spinning reel.
usos_embarcacion: Heavy jigging, deep bottom fishing and trolling: overhead reel or large saltwater spinning reel.
fichas.ojo: At sea, it must be a reel built for salt water: freshwater reels corrode in no time.

fichas.nombre: Reel size: when to use a 2500, a 3000, a 5000…
fichas.para: Which size of spinning reel to choose for each type of fishing.
fichas.resumen: The reel's number indicates its size and how much line it holds. Rule of thumb: smaller the finer the line and the lighter the lures; bigger for long casting, thick lines and hard-pulling fish.
como_es: Within a brand, higher number = bigger reel, more line and more drag.
Across brands it's not the same: one brand's 4000 can be quite a bit smaller than another's. Compare line capacity and maximum drag.
Daiwa standardised its LT sizes (spool diameter) as 1000, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000 and 6000.
The reel must balance the rod: a very big reel on a light rod tires your wrist.

fichas.nombre: The reel drag: how to set it
fichas.para: How tight to set the drag so you don't snap the line or lose the fish.
fichas.resumen: The general rule is to set it to roughly a quarter of the line's breaking strain (or the leader's, if it's weaker). With braid, a bit less.
como_es: Measure it with a spring balance (or luggage scale), pulling the line through the guides with the rod bent.
With nylon: around 20 % of the line's strength on fine lines and 25–30 % on heavy lines.
With braid: less (15 to 25 %), because it doesn't stretch and the full shock gets through.
Calculate it on the weakest link: the leader, the knot or the rod.
medidas: Example: 10 kg leader → drag around 2–2.5 kg.
usos_costa: Spinning with fine braid: light drag, the leader is the limit.
Surfcasting: a bit tighter to set the hook at distance, without overdoing it.
usos_embarcacion: Jigging and trolling: set it before you start and don't adjust it blindly with a fish on.
fichas.ojo: Don't tighten the drag by hand while the fish is pulling: that's when most lines break. Sources disagree on whether to back it off when storing the reel.

fichas.para: How to look after your tackle after sea fishing so it lasts for years.
fichas.resumen: Salt is the enemy: a gentle rinse with fresh water after every trip, drying well and a drop of lubricant prevent almost all breakdowns.
como_es: After every trip: rinse rod and reel with gentle fresh water, as a light shower or with a cloth. Never with a pressure jet or submerged: that drives the salt inside.
Dry everything well before storing; don't store it in a wet bag.
Check the guides: run a cotton bud round them; if it catches, there's a crack that will cut the line.
Clean the reel seat, where salt builds up.
Now and then, a thin coat of anti-corrosion protector or lubricant on the external metal parts (never on the drag).
Once a year, a reel service at a shop, or strip it down yourself if you know how.
medidas: Rinse: every trip. Full service: once a year (or sooner if it's noisy or turns stiffly).
usos_costa: After beach fishing, the sand: also rinse the reel's bail arm and rotor.
usos_embarcacion: On a boat, spray gets on everything all day: always rinse when you get back.
fichas.ojo: Don't use strong soap or solvents on the reel: they remove the grease inside. And don't put oil on the drag.

Large spinning reel with a long, tapered spool (long cast).
Fine main line to fly further and a shock leader to take the strain of the cast.

fichas.resumen: Light, sensitive rod with a medium spinning reel and braid: you'll cast thousands of times, so weight matters.

Medium spinning reel with a good drag.
Fine braid with a fluorocarbon leader.

High-capacity overhead reel with lever or star drag.
Rod holders on the boat: the rod works on its own until the strike.

fichas.para: A prawn-shaped lure with a crown of barbless pins at the tail, for squid and cuttlefish.
fichas.resumen: Cast it, let it sink and make it dart with sharp lifts: squid attack it as it falls. It is the way to catch squid from harbours and rocks.
como_es: Prawn-shaped body, often cloth-covered; a crown of barbless pins behind.
There are sinking (standard), floating and slow-sinking «shallow» models for shallow water.
Sizes are numbers (2.5, 3.0, 3.5…): a 2.5 is about 7.5 cm long and a 3.5 about 10.5 cm.
Sink rate is given in seconds per metre (standard models, about 3–3.5 s/m).
medidas: 2.5: small squid, shallow and calm water.
3.0: the most used all-rounder.
3.5: deeper water, current or big squid.
Check the weight and sink rate on the packet: they vary a lot between models.
usos_costa: At night under harbour and breakwater lights, or at dawn and dusk.
Cast, count it down, make two or three sharp lifts and let it fall again on a slack line.
usos_embarcacion: Slow drifting or anchored over sand and weed.
With lights at night, where allowed.
fichas.ojo: Your rod must handle the jig's weight. Carry different colours: the one that works changes from day to day.

fichas.para: A rig with several hooks dressed with feathers or shiny strips, with a lead or a jig at the end.
fichas.resumen: The classic way to catch mackerel and horse mackerel when they come in shoals: it imitates a small shoal of fish. The sabiki is the version with smaller hooks.
como_es: Feathers: 3 to 6 dressed hooks about 30 cm apart.
Sabiki: 6 to 10 small hooks, for small horse mackerel, sardine or bogue.
At the end, a lead or, better, a small bright jig.
A glow stick on the rig helps from a pier at night.

Big feathers for mackerel; sabiki for horse mackerel and small baitfish.
